units.title: Abstract state-machine specifications: variables, initial state and next-state relation
outcomes: Write a TLA+ state-machine spec with named state variables, an `Init` predicate and a `Next` action, and state what each variable abstracts away.
Run TLC on a finite model and report the constant assignment with every result.
Distinguish the specification from any implementation, and say which details the spec deliberately omits.
units.why: Model checking explores a spec, not code. If you cannot write variables plus Init plus Next, every later check in this section has nothing to run on.

next.note: Attach invariants and liveness claims to the spec shape from this unit.
Check a real commit-protocol spec with the same TLC loop.

study.title: Lecture 4: Die Hard
study.locator: Full lecture (19:39): write the water-jugs spec and check it with the parser and TLC
study.depth: Read the corrections page at https://lamport.azurewebsites.net/video/corrections.html for lectures 1, 3 and 4 before you run anything.

focus: A spec is variables plus `Init` plus `Next`. `Init` constrains the starting state; each disjunct of `Next` constrains one step as a relation between unprimed and primed variables.
An action that never mentions a variable leaves it unconstrained. `UNCHANGED vars` is what keeps the rest of the state still.
TLC checks a finite model, not the spec in general. Every constant needs a model value, or TLC cannot start.
The variables choose the abstraction. The Die Hard variables record jug contents, not jug hardware, pour durations or arm movements.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write a two-jug spec skeleton from memory: variables, `Init`, one pour action with primed assignments and `UNCHANGED` where needed, and run TLC to an explicit `No error has been found` result with the bound stated.
traps: Reading `x' = x + 1` as assignment. It is a constraint on the step; anything the action does not constrain may change arbitrarily.
Running TLC with an unassigned constant and reading the outcome as a result. An unbounded model is not a checked model.
Quoting `No error has been found` without the bound. The sentence is only true with the constant assignment attached.

selfTest.q: What are the three parts of a TLA+ state-machine spec, and what does each constrain?
selfTest.a: State variables hold the state. `Init` constrains the starting state. `Next` constrains each step as a relation between the current and the next state, usually run as `Init /\ [][Next]_vars`.

selfTest.q: An action sets `x' = 1` and never mentions `y`. What values can `y` take in the next state?
selfTest.a: Any value in its type. Unmentioned variables are unconstrained; add `UNCHANGED y` to keep it still.

selfTest.q: TLC prints `No error has been found` for your jugs spec. What exactly have you established?
selfTest.a: That the checked properties hold on the explored finite model only. The claim must name the constant assignment, for example the jug capacities and the pour bound.

selfTest.q: Why does the Die Hard spec record water levels rather than pour events?
selfTest.a: The variables fix the abstraction level. Levels are what the goal and the pour rule talk about; hardware and timing are deliberately omitted.

units.title: Safety invariants, liveness properties and fairness assumptions
outcomes: Separate a delivery claim into its safety half (nothing bad happens) and its liveness half (something good eventually happens).
Name the fairness assumption each liveness claim needs, and say which starvation it rules out.
Predict whether TLC can check a claim on a finite model, and what must be added when it cannot.
units.why: Safety without liveness accepts a system that does nothing; liveness without fairness blames the protocol for a starved scheduler. The alternating-bit protocol is the smallest system where both halves bite.

next.note: See how fairness and liveness survive when one spec implements another.
Check safety on a commit protocol, where liveness is deliberately left out.

study.title: Lecture 8 part 1: temporal formulas
study.locator: Full part (15:53): temporal formulas and what implementation will mean

study.title: Lecture 9 part 1: the high-level alternating-bit spec
study.locator: Full part (20:51): ABSpec.tla in video9a.zip, with `FairSpec == Spec /\ WF_vars(Next)` and the `Inv` invariant
study.depth: Download video9a.zip from the lecture page for ABSpec.tla; read it beside the video, not instead of it.

study.title: Lecture 9 part 2: the protocol and its fairness
study.locator: Full part (18:45): AB.tla in video9b.zip, with `Next == ASnd \/ ARcv \/ BSnd \/ BRcv \/ LoseMsg` and `FairSpec` adding `SF_vars(ARcv)`, `SF_vars(BRcv)`, `WF_vars(ASnd)`, `WF_vars(BSnd)`
study.depth: Read the corrections note for lecture 9 part 2 at https://lamport.azurewebsites.net/video/corrections.html first; it changes what the video says.

focus: Safety is checkable on finite prefixes: a duplication or a conflicting decision shows up in a bounded trace. Liveness needs infinite behaviors, so TLC needs fairness in the spec.
Fairness constrains the scheduler, not the algorithm. `WF_vars(ASnd)` says a persistently enabled send keeps happening; `SF_vars(ARcv)` says a repeatedly enabled receive keeps happening.
Loss is an action like any other. `LoseMsg` stays enabled forever, so delivery depends on resends plus fairness, not on the absence of loss.
The two specs separate concerns: ABSpec states what delivery means, AB states how retransmission with alternating bits achieves it under fairness.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the AB `Next` disjunction and the four fairness conjuncts of its `FairSpec` from memory, and explain which starvation each conjunct rules out.
traps: Adding fairness to silence a liveness violation without reading the trace. If the violating behavior is already fair, the protocol is wrong and fairness hides nothing.
Writing a liveness claim as a state predicate. `BVar = AVar` holds or not at a state; eventual delivery is a claim about the whole behavior.
Checking liveness with unbounded queues. `AtoB` and `BtoA` grow without bound, so TLC needs a queue-length constraint before it can finish.

selfTest.q: Split `every sent value is eventually received, and no value is received twice` into safety and liveness.
selfTest.a: No-duplicates is safety: one duplicated delivery in a finite prefix violates it. Eventual receipt is liveness: no finite prefix can show a value is never delivered.

selfTest.q: What does `FairSpec` add over `Spec` in AB.tla, and why?
selfTest.a: Four fairness conjuncts: strong fairness on the two receives and weak fairness on the two sends. They rule out behaviors where an enabled send or receive is starved forever, which liveness needs.

selfTest.q: TLC reports a liveness violation whose trace shows the sender never sending. Is the protocol broken?
selfTest.a: Not shown. The behavior starves `ASnd`; add `WF_vars(ASnd)` first. Only a violation of the fair spec indicts the protocol.

selfTest.q: Why do the AB model runs need a queue-length bound such as `Len(AtoB) <= 3`?
selfTest.a: The message queues are unbounded sequences, so the state space is infinite. The bound makes the model finite; results hold only within it.

units.title: Implementation versus specification refinement, nondeterminism and environment actions
outcomes: Explain implementation as behavior inclusion: every visible behavior below is a behavior above, with internal steps as stuttering.
Place nondeterministic choices and environment actions (loss, crash, abort) in the spec, and say what a check omits when they are missing.
Read a refinement claim such as `TPSpec => TC!TCSpec` and name which variables are hidden.
units.why: Testing compares outputs; refinement compares behaviors. It is the only precise meaning of `this protocol implements that commit abstraction` in this section.

next.note: See the TwoPhase-to-TCommit refinement checked on a finite model.
Reuse the safety-versus-liveness split for state-machine replication.

study.locator: Full part (12:13): what it means for one specification to implement another

study.title: Refinement
study.locator: The refinement topic: when one spec implements another; read after lecture 8 part 2

study.title: Lecture 15: Verification of distributed systems (IronFleet)
study.locator: Refinement through Inductive invariants sections: IronFleet-style refinement, externally visible events, stuttering, transitivity, and why a wrong middle layer proves nothing

focus: Refinement is behavior inclusion on visible state. The low-level spec may take internal steps; above, they look like stuttering.
High-level nondeterminism is implementation freedom. TCommit lets a prepared transaction commit or abort; TwoPhase may always abort and still refine it.
The environment is part of the model. TwoPhase has `RMChooseToAbort` and spontaneous `TMAbort`; AB has `LoseMsg`. A missing environment action is an unchecked assumption.
Refinement is transitive but garbage-preserving: the IronFleet lecture shows a wrong protocol layer gets stuck at the next refinement step, not excused by the one below.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, explain the claim `TPSpec => TC!TCSpec`: what it says, which variables the TCommit side sees (`rmState` only), and why always-abort still refines the abstract commit.
traps: Proving impl-to-protocol and stopping. The IronFleet lecture's election-restriction question shows the stuck proof appears at the protocol-to-spec step.
Calling a nondeterministic spec random. Nondeterminism is arbitrary choice explored by the checker, not a distribution the system samples.
Hiding state the property reads. `tmPrepared` and `msgs` can hide because `TCConsistent` only reads `rmState`; hiding `rmState` itself would void the claim.

selfTest.q: What does `TPSpec => TC!TCSpec` assert?
selfTest.a: Every behavior of the TwoPhase commit protocol is a behavior of the abstract Transaction Commit spec: 2PC implements commit, including the `TCConsistent` invariant that no two RMs decide in conflict.

selfTest.q: TwoPhase refines TCommit. May a conforming implementation abort every transaction?
selfTest.a: Yes. TCommit's `Decide` permits abort while nothing committed, so always-abort behaviors satisfy the abstract spec. Refinement permits useless but safe implementations.

selfTest.q: In the IronFleet lecture, where does a wrong protocol layer get caught?
selfTest.a: At the protocol-to-spec refinement step. Impl-to-protocol may still prove; the wrong middle layer gets stuck against the trusted top spec.

selfTest.q: Why is the proof untrusted but the specification and the checker trusted?
selfTest.a: The checker mechanically re-verifies the proof, so a bad proof is caught. Nothing re-verifies the spec, so a wrong spec certifies a wrong system.

study.title: TwoPhase.tla and TCommit.tla with TwoPhase.cfg
study.locator: TwoPhase.tla (variables `rmState`, `tmState`, `tmPrepared`, `msgs`; actions `TMCommit`, `TMAbort`, `RMPrepare`, `RMChooseToAbort`, `RMRcvCommitMsg`, `RMRcvAbortMsg`; `TPSpec == TPInit /\ [][TPNext]_vars`) with TwoPhase.cfg (`RM = {r1, r2, r3}`, invariant `TPTypeOK`, `SPECIFICATION TPSpec`)
study.depth: Do not open `specifications/TwoPhase/` elsewhere in the repo: it is a hardware handshake, not transaction commit.

focus: The header states the scope honestly: safety only, what is allowed. Liveness (what must happen) is not specified, so a run that commits nothing violates nothing.
Messages are never removed from `msgs`. Receipt is existence in the set, so duplicates are allowed and loss is modeled as never receiving.
`TMCommit` needs `tmPrepared = RM`; `TMAbort` needs nothing but `tmState = init`. The asymmetry is the blocking window: a prepared RM waits for a decision that may never come.
The checked theorems are `TPSpec => []TPTypeOK` and `TPSpec => TC!TCSpec`. Type correctness and refinement to abstract commit, both within the configured bound.
units.reproduce: From the Examples directory, run TLC on TwoPhase.cfg unchanged and get `1146 states generated, 288 distinct states found` at depth 11 with `No error has been found`. Then assert a false invariant and read the violating trace to the committing action.
traps: Running TLC without a bound and calling the wait a result. A spec without assigned finite constants runs until killed; the bound is part of the result.
Reading `No error has been found` as proved. It covers three resource managers and the configured invariant only; the file notes a separate six-RM check with 50816 reachable states.
Confusing `specifications/TwoPhase/` with `specifications/transaction_commit/TwoPhase.tla`. The first is a hardware handshake and its model needs the TLAPS module to parse.

selfTest.q: What does `TMCommit` require, and what does `TMAbort` require?
selfTest.a: Commit needs `tmState = init` and `tmPrepared = RM`, every manager prepared. Abort needs only `tmState = init`: the TM may abort spontaneously at any time before committing.

selfTest.q: A prepared RM never receives a Commit or Abort message. Which property is violated?
selfTest.a: None in this spec. It specifies safety only; the blocking wait is allowed. The violation would be against an unstated liveness claim.

selfTest.q: What does a TLC trace line `State 4: <RMPrepare ...>` tell you?
selfTest.a: That step 4 applied the `RMPrepare` action, with the file and column range shown, and the `/\ var = value` lines below give the full state after the step.

selfTest.q: Your run reports 288 distinct states for three RMs. What changes with six RMs, and what stays the same?
selfTest.a: The state count grows (the file notes 50816 reachable states); the spec text and the invariant are unchanged. Each bound is its own result.

selfTest.q: What is `TCConsistent`, and which spec states it?
selfTest.a: No two RMs in conflicting decisions (`aborted` versus `committed`), stated in TCommit.tla and asserted as `THEOREM TCSpec => [](TCTypeOK /\ TCConsistent)`.

study.title: Replicated Log and Stream Processor: protocol specification
study.locator: Protocol and state-machine specification and invariants deliverable: the spec contract your model must satisfy

focus: Reduce before you specify. Model one partition's log with a fixed manager set first; multi-partition and membership changes are later extensions, each with its own TLC run.
Committed means what your spec says it means. Name the commit point (majority acknowledgment, leader decision) as an action, not as prose.
Every extension re-runs TLC. A passing run before the extension says nothing about the model after it.
Keep the first meaningful counterexample per extension. A trace that changed the spec is evidence; a final green run alone is not.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, write Init and Next for a single-decree commit with two resource managers, bound it, and run TLC to a stated distinct-state count with `No error has been found`.
traps: Specifying the whole capstone at once. State explosion will end the run before it teaches anything; one partition and three managers finish in under a second.
Modeling the network as reliable by omission. If loss, duplication and reorder are not actions, TLC cannot find the bugs they cause.
Polishing away the failing trace. The first counterexample is the unit's main artifact; keep it with the bound that produced it.

selfTest.q: What belongs in the first version of your log spec?
selfTest.a: One partition, a fixed manager set, log plus epoch plus commit-index variables, append and commit actions, and the committed-entries-preserved invariant. Everything else is a later extension with its own run.

selfTest.q: Why does the pool's use note insist on running TLC after every extension?
selfTest.a: Each extension changes the state space. A green run on the smaller model does not cover the larger one.

selfTest.q: What does the AWS paper's findings table actually show?
selfTest.a: Per-component spec sizes (for example an 804-line PlusCal model) beside the bugs each model found (two bugs for that one). It shows models find bugs; it does not set a bugs-per-line rate.

selfTest.q: Your spec passes with three managers. What may you claim about five?
selfTest.a: Nothing. A larger bound is a new check; report each bound with its own count.

units.title: State-based and operation-based CRDT requirements and one CRDT implementation
outcomes: State the state-based convergence requirements (join-semilattice merge: commutative, associative, idempotent) and the operation-based delivery requirements (causal order with each operation applied once).
Prove the operation-based map CRDT converges and sketch its multi-value variant.
Implement one CRDT (G-Counter or OR-Set) with merge-law and convergence tests.
units.why: CRDTs are the one replication design that converges without consensus. Their requirements are exact strength: drop idempotence or causal delivery and convergence silently goes.

next.note: Use the convergence-proof vocabulary for causal and eventual consistency histories.
See where active-active regions pay the CRDT metadata and conflict costs.

study.title: Shapiro et al. 2011, Sections 1 to 3
study.locator: Sections 1 to 3: state-based and operation-based definitions, the join-semilattice merge laws and the delivery conditions, plus one example type for your implementation
study.depth: Read one example type only (G-Counter or OR-Set), not the whole catalog.

study.title: Section 8.1: collaboration and conflict resolution
study.locator: Section 8.1 (pp. 78-80): the operation-based map CRDT over reliable broadcast, the state-based map with merge operator t on Slide 146, and Exercises 21 and 22

study.title: HLD Handbook: CRDTs chapter
study.locator: State-based (CvRDT) merge as least upper bound with the G-Counter elementwise-max code, op-based (CmRDT) over causal broadcast with the op-based OR-Set tag diagram, and the tombstone and metadata cost section
study.depth: Use the chapter for implementation texture (delta-state CRDTs, reported Automerge figures). The requirements come from Shapiro and Kleppmann, not from here.

focus: State-based convergence needs three merge laws: commutative, associative, idempotent. Elementwise max on per-replica counters satisfies all three; that is the whole G-Counter argument.
Operation-based convergence needs reliable causal delivery plus commuting operations plus exactly-once application. The broadcast carries the requirement, not the data structure.
Unique tags decide remove semantics. An OR-Set remove only removes observed tags, so a concurrent add with a fresh tag survives.
Tombstones and identifiers are the price. Removals that must survive late arrivals keep metadata forever; size it before promising scale.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, merge `{A: 3}` with `{B: 2, C: 5}` by elementwise max to `{A: 3, B: 2, C: 5}` with value \(3 + 2 + 5 = 10\), and state which merge law covers reorder, merge-of-merges and redelivery.
traps: Running state-based merge over a lossy channel and calling it op-based. State merge tolerates loss by idempotence; operation delivery does not tolerate loss or reorder without the broadcast guarantees.

Reading the HLD op-based section as two delivery modes. It states one requirement: causal order with duplicate suppression so each operation applies once. The transport alone does not give the second half.
Forgetting the tombstone set in a 2P-Set-style remove. A removed element re-added without fresh identity resurrects or vanishes depending on which replica you ask.

selfTest.q: State the three merge laws and the fault each one absorbs.
selfTest.a: Commutative (reorder), associative (merge-of-merges regrouping), idempotent (duplication and redelivery). All three are needed for convergence over an arbitrary transport.

selfTest.q: Why does the operation-based map need reliable broadcast while the state-based map works over best-effort broadcast?
selfTest.a: State merge is idempotent, so repeats and loss are harmless. Operations must each arrive once and in causal order; the notes state state-based merge tolerates loss because the merge operator is idempotent, while op-based requires reliable broadcast.

selfTest.q: Two replicas hold `{A: 3}` and `{B: 2, C: 5}`. What is the merged state and its value?
selfTest.a: `{A: 3, B: 2, C: 5}` with value \(3 + 2 + 5 = 10\): elementwise max, then the sum.

selfTest.q: A remove and a concurrent add of `x` race in an OR-Set. Does `x` survive?
selfTest.a: Yes. The remove carries only observed tags; the concurrent add uses a fresh tag the remove never saw, so the merge keeps the new tagged entry.

selfTest.q: What does Exercise 22 change relative to the last-writer-wins map?
selfTest.a: Concurrent updates for a key keep all values (multi-value register semantics) instead of only the greatest timestamp; the reader returns the set.

study.title: Chapter 9: Formal Methods and Randomized Testing
study.locator: Printed pp. 384-387: property-based testing, fuzzing and deterministic simulation testing as the empirical half beside proofs, and why model and implementation can drift apart

focus: `Bundle`s build the universe of values rules share. Generating fresh keys per rule rarely collides; drawing from a bundle forces the overwrites and deletes that find bugs.
The invariant runs after every step. It compares system against model on the same operation history, so the first failing step is already localized.
Shrinking deletes what does not matter. The docs' five-step program (new key, new value, save, delete, check) is the minimal story: keep it, it is the regression test.
A seed makes a schedule replayable. Record the seed with every failure; a failure without its seed is an anecdote.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, write a key-value log versus dict machine with new-key, put and delete rules plus an after-every-step invariant, plant a delete bug, and paste the shrunk failing program.
traps: Asserting inside rules instead of invariants. A rule assertion checks one path; an invariant checks every interleaving the generator produces.
Using `assume` to skip inapplicable states. Sparse assumptions starve the generator; `precondition` filters rules before generation instead.
Keeping the passing run and deleting the planted-bug demo. The bug demo is what proves the machine can catch its fault class.

selfTest.q: Why do the docs use `Bundle`s for keys and values instead of generating fresh ones per rule?
selfTest.a: Bundles build a shared universe, so later rules reuse earlier values. Fresh generation rarely collides, which hides the overwrite and delete interactions that find bugs.

selfTest.q: What does the shrinker output for the planted delete bug, and why keep it?
selfTest.a: A minimal program: new key, new value, save, delete, check. It is the regression test: short, deterministic and readable.

selfTest.q: When should `stateful_step_count` go up and `max_examples` go down?
selfTest.a: When hunting ordering bugs that need long setups: longer programs per example, fewer examples overall. The docs' example doubles steps to 100 and halves examples to 50.

selfTest.q: A seeded schedule fails once and passes on rerun with a new seed. What do you keep?
selfTest.a: The failing seed and the schedule it produced. Without the seed the failure cannot be replayed, and the fix cannot be verified against it.

practice.name: Hypothesis stateful docs: extend the DatabaseComparison machine
practice.locator: `DatabaseComparison` with keys and values bundles: add a third rule of your own, plant a one-line model bug, and keep the shrunk failing program
practice.note: Run on the installed Hypothesis (6.169.1 here); record the version with the trace.

practice.name: FoundationDB paper: sketch your deterministic scheduler
practice.locator: Simulation-testing section: implement delay, drop, duplicate, reorder and crash operations behind a fixed seed in your own log harness
practice.note: Copy the pattern (seeded RNG, replayable schedule), not the system. The scheduler itself is section mini-project infrastructure.

fit.note: The Hypothesis state-machine reference plus the FoundationDB scheduler model and the DDIA testing vocabulary cover property and schedule exploration at implement depth with two named builds.

units.title: Operation-history normalization and linearizability checker scope
outcomes: Record operation histories with invocation and completion times, process ids, function names and return values.
Normalize client observations into a checker-ready history and run a single-register linearizability check on fixed histories.
State the checker's scope: what a clean run establishes and what it cannot prove.
units.why: A checker verdict is only as good as the history it reads. Normalization turns ambiguous client observations into the exact object the model reasons about.

next.note: Embed the checker in a full generator, client, nemesis and checker campaign.
Reuse the history vocabulary for linearizability versus sequential consistency.

study.title: Consistency Models map: histories and operations
study.locator: Systems, Processes, Operations and Invocation and Completion Times sections: the operation as invoke/ok pairs with function names and values, and the single-object hierarchy (linearizable implies sequential implies causal)
study.depth: Read the map for vocabulary and the hierarchy arrows. The availability coloring is Jepsen's summary of known results, not a measurement.

study.title: Chapter 10: Linearizability
study.locator: Printed pp. 402-410: what makes a system linearizable, the recency guarantee and history classification
study.depth: Review only: rebuild from your DS-4 consistency units and point back to them by title instead of re-reading at full depth.

focus: A history is invoke/ok pairs per process with function names and values. Timeless logs without completion markers cannot be checked.
Normalization resolves ambiguity before checking: failed and crashed operations become explicit outcomes; retries become separate invocations with their identity preserved.
Knossos checks one register against `knossos.model/register`. A stale read (write 2 completes, later read returns 1) is invalid; multi-object claims need a different checker.
A clean run is bounded evidence. It says these histories show no violation of this model; it is not a proof of the system.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the two fixed histories (write-then-read returning the written value; write-2-then-read-returning-1) and the expected Knossos verdicts (`valid? true`; `valid? false`).
traps: Feeding a plain vector where a history object is required. Checkers assert on well-formed invoke/ok structures; a malformed input fails your harness, not the system.
Checking a multi-key workload with a single-register model. The model verdict says nothing about the keys it never saw.
Presenting a clean run as serializability. A linearizability check on one register cannot establish a multi-object isolation claim.

selfTest.q: What four fields does each history entry need, and why?
selfTest.a: Process, type (invoke/ok/fail), function and value. The checker needs per-process order plus invocation-completion pairing to test real-time order.

selfTest.q: Write 2 completes, then a read returns 1. What is the verdict under the register model?
selfTest.a: Invalid. The read completed after write 2 completed but returned the older value, violating recency. Verified: `valid? false`.

selfTest.q: Why must retries keep their identity through normalization?
selfTest.a: A retried write that ran twice is one logical operation with two attempts. Dropping the link double-counts effects or hides the duplicate the checker should see.

selfTest.q: Knossos reports valid on your history. What may you claim?
selfTest.a: That this history shows no single-register linearizability violation. Not that the system is linearizable, and nothing about other objects or longer histories.

practice.name: Jepsen Knossos: check two fixed single-register histories
practice.locator: `knossos.core/analysis` with `knossos.model/register` on the write-then-read history (expect `valid? true`) and the stale-read history (expect `valid? false`)
practice.note: Run from any Clojure runtime with Knossos on the classpath. Record the version beside the verdicts; describe only what these two histories check.

units.stopWhen: Both fixed histories return the predicted verdicts, and you can state the object, the model and the completeness limit of each run in one sentence.

fit.note: The Jepsen history vocabulary plus the DDIA linearizability sections and the two fixed Knossos runs cover normalization and checker scope at implement depth.

units.title: Jepsen generator, client, nemesis and checker roles and a fault and workload coverage matrix
outcomes: Name the four Jepsen roles (generator, client, nemesis, checker) and what each produces or consumes.
Run an Elle `rw-register` check on two fixed transaction histories and read the anomaly types.
Draft a fault and workload coverage matrix: faults down one side, workloads across the top, checker per cell.
units.why: A fault campaign without named roles is a pile of scripts. The four roles turn `test under faults` into a repeatable design with a checker verdict per cell.

next.note: Aim the campaign at a reconstructed real system instead of your own log.
File every campaign history as raw evidence with its checker verdict.

study.title: Jepsen framework roles at v0.3.14
study.locator: `client.clj` (the `Client` protocol), `nemesis.clj` (the `Nemesis` protocol), `checker.clj`, and `generator/interpreter.clj` (interprets pure-generator operations, spawns worker threads, records the history)

study.title: Elle: Inferring Isolation Anomalies (Kingsbury and Alvaro)
study.locator: Abstract and Sections 1-2 (arXiv v1, 23 March 2020): black-box isolation checking from client observations, Adya-style dependency-graph inference, the soundness claim and the completeness requirement on histories
study.depth: Elle detects the Adya anomalies except predicates, one pattern per checker run. A clean run needs complete histories and still is not a proof.

focus: The generator produces the operation schedule; the client executes it against the system; the nemesis injects faults on a schedule of its own; the checker reads the recorded history. Histories, not logs, are the handoff between them.
Elle infers version order from what reads observed. List-append and read-write-register workloads reveal versions; opaque values reveal nothing, so workload design is checker design.
Anomaly types name the violation: `:G1a` is an aborted read (reading data from a transaction that never committed). Read the type before the graph.
The matrix is the coverage claim. An empty cell is an untested combination; say so instead of letting the campaign imply it.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the two Elle histories (committed-write-then-read; aborted-write-then-read) and the expected verdicts (`valid? true`; `valid? false` with `:G1a`), and sketch a 3-by-3 fault and workload matrix with a checker per cell.
traps: Starting the JVM without headless mode for Elle. `elle.core` touches AWT; without `-Djava.awt.headless=true` it throws instead of checking anything.
Passing a plain vector as the history. Elle asserts on a real history object (`jepsen.history/history`); the not-history error is your bug, not a system result.
Calling `elle.core/check` with bare model options on a hand-built history. It throws a null-analyzer error; use the model-specific entry (`elle.rw-register/check`) instead.

selfTest.q: What does each Jepsen role hand to the next?
selfTest.a: The generator hands operation schedules to clients; clients hand request and response pairs (the history) to the checker; the nemesis independently hands fault schedules to the environment. The checker reads histories, never live systems.

selfTest.q: What is a `:G1a` anomaly in one sentence?
selfTest.a: An aborted read: a transaction observed a value written by a transaction that aborted (or never committed). The fixed history shows a `:fail` write followed by a read returning its value.

selfTest.q: Why does Elle need list-append or read-write-register workloads rather than opaque writes?
selfTest.a: It infers version order from what reads return. Values must reveal their version history; opaque values give the inference nothing to work with.

selfTest.q: Your matrix has an empty partition-plus-snapshot-isolation cell. What do you report?
selfTest.a: An untested combination. The campaign covers only filled cells; the empty one is a stated gap, not a pass.

practice.name: Elle rw-register check on two fixed histories
practice.locator: `elle.rw-register/check` over `jepsen.history/history` objects: committed-write-then-read (expect `valid? true`) and aborted-write-then-read (expect `valid? false` with `(:G1a :empty-transaction-graph)`)
practice.note: Start the JVM with `-Djava.awt.headless=true`. Keep both verdicts; the matrix in Reproduce gets one checker per cell from this pattern.

units.stopWhen: Both Elle histories return the predicted verdicts with the anomaly type read correctly, and your matrix names a checker for every filled cell and marks the empty ones.

fit.note: The pinned Jepsen roles plus the Elle paper and the two fixed rw-register runs cover campaign roles and fault coverage at explain and implement depth.
